summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the new Penal Code, in force since 2018, provides an equal age of consent regardless of sex, while retaining higher penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex.

Benin law provides no prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and no protection against discrimination based on gender identity in particular. Legal gender recognition is impossible, so a trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection to invoke.

Benin does not recognise LGBTQI+ couples and families. The sole exception sourced is the grant of diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children’s Code, Law 2015-08, bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption.

The United States State Department 2023 human rights report found hostility toward LGBTQI+ persons, most pronounced outside major urban areas, with routine refusal of medical care, including hormone treatment, and of social services. Other sources report regular refusal of LGBTQ-related care such as gender-affirming hormone therapy and regular denial of general care such as malaria treatment.

Physical danger comes principally from private actors. Reports describe anti-gay lynchings as commonplace, alongside arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment. Violence is described as mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities, while police rarely pursue perpetrators.

Victims conceal sexual orientation or gender identity when reporting violence or discrimination for fear of mistreatment by police. Lesbian, bisexual and queer women are reported to rarely report to police, indicating no reliable protection machinery for a visitor who needs help.

A narrow set of electronic and data rules exists. Article 552 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code, in place since 2018, punishes provocation of discrimination, hatred or violence based on sexual orientation through an electronic communications network or computer system with one year of imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, or one of those penalties only. Article 394 of the same law and Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law prohibit processing personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, the latter without express consent. Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 of 2012 requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts or behaviour based on sex or real or perceived sexuality that infringe the rights and dignity of women or girls.

Enforcement history qualifies the legal status. Benin’s representative stated in the 2008 review that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered under the provisions then on the books. The general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct. Benin rejected recommendations to improve the situation of LGBTQ persons in the 2012 review. In the 2023 Universal Periodic Review the government accepted two of fifteen recommendations concerning LGBTQ persons, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against persons living with HIV.

Religious institutions contribute to hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries. Priests are documented as calling transgender people demons. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques take part in homophobic preaching. Imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion practices, often coerced by families.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Benin. Public events have nevertheless occurred, including a public International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event organised by LGBTQ associations in Cotonou at the Institut Français on 17 May 2013, attended by 200 people.

Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restriction for LGBT people.

Since about 2020 the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has operated temporary accommodation reported as 20 places, through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region passed by 2024. The scale of that caseload relative to capacity underlines the level of social violence, while the facility itself is youth shelter infrastructure rather than a visitor service.
tangentialFactors:
Earlier penal texts illustrate the path to the current position. Article 331 of the old Penal Code, with a 1947 amendment, punished an indecent act or act against nature with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years of imprisonment and a fine of 200 to 50,000 francs. Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent act or act against nature with a person of the same sex with one to three years of imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs, but it was never voted into law. The October 2008 draft contained no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and has not been voted on.

Social attitudes described in the sources frame homosexuality as unnatural and foreign. Homosexuality is reported as perceived as stemming from Western culture, with homosexuals described as deviants and homosexuality described as a disease brought by white people.

A 31 August 2015 report commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups recorded LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describing discrimination and persecution from churches and governments. The date limits its value as evidence of current conditions in Benin.
localsOnly:
Anthropologist Patrick Awondo, cited in a 2012 interview, pointed to evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin, and Melville Herskovits recorded women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom on the territory of modern Benin. The account presents same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import.

Rejection by families is reported as frequent for LGBTQ people, with difficulty obtaining employment. Employers are reported as often unwilling to hire people known to be LGBTQ, with transgender and intersex people singled out.

While the government provides sexual and reproductive health care for people who experienced sexual violence, LGBTQ people are typically denied such care and other social services.

Conversion practices by imams, priests and traditional healers are often coerced by families, placing particular pressure on younger residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced for Benin are entry and visa rules as applied to a trans visitor, airport or other screening procedures that could risk outing, and any law on access to toilets or other sex-segregated facilities.

Unresolved is the current frequency or circumstances of use of the general indecency provision against same-sex conduct, beyond the sourced finding that it has been used.

Not sourced is any separate finding on societal tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general stigmatization of LGBTQ persons, beyond the two sourced points on hiring discrimination that singles out transgender and intersex people and on priests calling transgender people demons.

Unresolved is the practical scope of the diplomatic-partner visa and immunity exception, beyond the sourced finding that it is granted.

The 2015 finding on discrimination by churches and governments across four countries is not sourced as a current-state finding for Benin.
